name: The soul as form of the body, and the immortality of mind alone
plain_explanation: The soul is not a separate ghostly substance inside the body; it is what makes a body one organized, purposeful living thing -- the way a shape makes a lump of wax into a particular seal-impression. But within the soul, Aristotle distinguishes a higher part, 'mind,' which alone might survive the body's death.
precise_definition: In Aristotle's On the Soul, the soul is 'the actuality of a body' having life potentially within it -- related to the body as form to matter -- and is therefore, for the most part, inseparable from the body and perishes with it. Mind (nous), however, is described as 'an independent substance implanted within the soul,' timeless because its objects (mathematics, philosophy) are timeless, and 'incapable of being destroyed'; the Nicomachean Ethics adds that the rational soul's contemplative activity is the highest happiness, in which a person 'shares in the divine life' impersonally rather than as an individual.
why_it_mattered: It produced centuries of controversy (Averroes and his followers held Aristotle taught no personal immortality at all) and set the template for later distinctions between an animating 'soul' and a separately immortal 'intellect' or 'reason.'
historical_origin: Developed across Aristotle's On the Soul and Nicomachean Ethics.
examples: The eye cannot see when parted from the body, illustrating that an organ's purpose (and hence the soul's work) depends on the living organic whole
Self-nutrition as the only psychic power possessed by plants, versus sensation and motivity in animals, versus thought in the part of humans called 'mind'
competing_positions: The Pythagorean doctrine of transmigration of souls, which Aristotle explicitly ridicules
Averroes's interpretation that Aristotle taught no immortality at all -- a reading Dante associated with the 'Epicureans' he places in hell
influence_on_later_thinkers: Because mind, for Aristotle, is impersonal and shared rather than individual, Russell concludes that on the most natural reading its 'immortality' is not personal survival but a shared participation in the divine -- 'if he succeeded completely, he would have ceased to exist as a separate person.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Closely tied to Aristotle's theology, since mind's timeless objects link it to the divine, unmoved mover.
